outputs.L3:
# On the Impossibility of Safety: Reading Black Masculinity Against Media Caricature

The author's work stands as a deliberate rejection of the reductive, media-manufactured images of Black masculinity that saturate American popular culture. He refuses the athletic imagery peddled by commercials—the hypermasculine, commodified Black body reduced to spectacle and sale. He similarly rejects the criminalized fashion codes that mainstream media has taught audiences to read as inherently threatening: the hoodie, the sagging pants, the do-rag, all signifiers weaponized against Black men regardless of the individuals wearing them. The "thug" caricature, with its accompanying assumptions of criminality and violence, is explicitly cast aside as a false and damaging narrative that the author refuses to inhabit or perform.

This refusal extends further into an explicit rejection of clichéd storylines that tether Black male identity to violence, gang affiliation, and the spectacle of courtroom drama or tabloid coverage. The text resists becoming another entry in the long catalog of racialized shootings turned into media events—cases where real human lives are transformed into cultural flashpoints, hashtags, and cautionary tales stripped of nuance. By naming and refusing these narratives, the author pushes back against the flattening of Black male experience into a single, endlessly repeated story of violence and victimhood.

Central to this critique is an incisive examination of "stand your ground" rhetoric and the vigilante logic it enables. The text conjures a "Clint Eastwood" figure—an emblem of American self-styled justice and rugged individualism—who perceives threat not in action but in mere presence. This figure feels endangered simply by the existence of a Black man in his vicinity, by the clothes he wears, by the space he occupies. This is the logic that has justified real violence: the notion that Blackness itself, unaccompanied by any actual aggression, constitutes sufficient grounds for lethal "self-defense." The poem exposes this rhetoric as a thin veneer over deeply embedded racial anxiety and violence.

In direct contrast to these looming caricatures, the speaker offers a self-portrait calibrated for maximum respectability: Dockers, a blazer, an Obama tie. This is armor of a different kind—not the armor of toughness but of assimilation, an attempt to signal safety, education, and belonging to dominant cultural norms. This sartorial choice illuminates W.E.B. Du Bois's concept of "double consciousness," the psychological split experienced by Black Americans who must constantly view themselves through the lens of a white gaze that presumes threat, even as they attempt to construct an identity of their own choosing. The speaker's careful dress becomes a performance staged for an audience whose scrutiny he cannot escape, a negotiation between authentic selfhood and defensive self-presentation.

Yet the poem's devastating conclusion undercuts this entire strategy of respectability politics. Despite the calculated, sanitized image the speaker has constructed—despite every effort to appear unthreatening, professional, aligned with symbols of racial progress like the Obama tie—the poem ends with a violent, visceral image: a lapel pin or flower "with his head blown off." This closing image serves as a brutal reminder that no amount of assimilation, no careful curation of dress or demeanor, can fully guarantee protection from racialized violence. The poem thus dismantles the myth that respectability is a shield, suggesting instead that the threat Black men face is not contingent on behavior or appearance but is embedded in a system that will find justification for violence regardless of how carefully one attempts to perform safety. The final image lingers as a somber acknowledgment of this reality—that the very effort to escape stereotype can itself become another site of vulnerability, another place where violence finds its target.
outputs.L4:
# What They See When They Don't See Me

I am not Iverson crossing over on the highlight reel,
not a Gatorade commercial sweat-dripped and slow-mo cool,
not the bass drop when the beat kicks in,
not a chain, not a hood, not a fist raised in a mugshot flash.

I am pressed khaki. I am Dockers crease sharp enough
to cut through the assumptions before they land.
I am the Obama tie, blue and red woven like a promise
nobody asked me to keep but I keep it anyway—
knotted tight at 6 AM, straightened twice in the mirror,
because somebody somewhere is already deciding
what my hands mean before I've used them for anything.

They want the du-rag. They want the low-slung jeans,
the swagger they can name and therefore tame,
therefore fear, therefore shoot first and call it instinct.
So I give them cardigan. I give them loafers.
I give them the version of myself sanded down
to fit inside a Werther's commercial,
inside a father-of-the-year mug,
inside anything that says *safe* in a language
they were taught before they could talk.

Watch me not wear the jersey.
Watch me not bounce the ball.
Watch me carry a briefcase like a shield
made of nothing, made of paper,
made of the same air that didn't save
Tamir, didn't save Trayvon,
didn't ask what he was wearing
before it asked what he was.

Because here's the thing they never tell you
about the tie, about the khakis, about
speaking three registers above suspicion:
none of it is armor. It's camouflage
for a war they never admit they're fighting.

I have seen a dandelion
pinned neat and yellow to an American lapel,
stem tucked in like a boutonniere,
bright as a badge, bright as a promise—
picked clean from someone's front yard,
grown wild and easy and low to the ground,
just trying to catch a little light—

with his head blown off.

You can dress the weed up nice.
You can call it a flower.
You can pin it to the finest coat in the closet.

The world will still find a way
to separate the bloom
from the body.
outputs.L5:
# The Rainbow on My Feet

I never expected a bag of candy to change how I felt about my sneakers, but that's exactly what happened last spring.

I'd been eyeing a pair of Nike trainers for weeks—the kind with that distinctive swoosh that somehow makes you walk a little taller. They weren't anything special in the grand scheme of footwear, just a clean design in white and grey, comfortable enough for both morning jogs and lazy afternoon errands. When I finally bought them, I felt an odd sense of accomplishment, like I'd achieved something rather than just made a purchase.

The Skittles connection came later, and somewhat by accident. I was walking home from the store with a bag of the candy, the kind you buy on impulse at the checkout line, when I noticed how the colors scattered across the pavement matched almost perfectly with a discoloration on my trainer's sole—a rainbow smudge from stepping in something colorful earlier that day. It struck me as funny: here I was, wearing shoes I'd saved up for, treating them with almost reverent care, and yet life had already left its mark.

There's something to be said about the relationship between the things we cherish and the mess of everyday living. My Nike trainers, despite their pristine appearance in the box, were destined to collect scuffs, grass stains, and mysterious rainbow-colored marks from candy-adjacent accidents. The Skittles themselves didn't survive the walk home; they became a small treat consumed on my porch steps, colors dissolving into simple sweetness.

Maybe that's the lesson in ordinary objects—trainers get worn, candy gets eaten, and both leave behind small evidence of a day lived rather than merely observed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a spoken-word poem about racial profiling that subverts athletic/media stereotypes of young Black men, using rapid-fire pop culture references and dark irony.
counterfactuals.output:
# Highlight Reel

They see the six-two frame and start the countdown clock—
ESPN in their eyes before I even talk,
already got my jersey number, my forty time,
they're scouting me for a combine I never signed up for in the first place.

Yo they love us in a highlight reel, hate us on a sidewalk,
love the crossover, fear the cross-walk,
they'll chant my name in a stadium of eighty thousand,
but that same throat closes up when I'm just standing
at a bus stop in a hoodie looking "suspicious"—
Vince Staples said it best, but let me get specific:

I'm not Kyrie, I'm not Trae,
I'm not a bag of skittles that Zimmerman saw as prey,
I'm not LeBron's chosen one, I'm not a Draft Day story,
I'm just trying to walk home without becoming an allegory.

Funny how they need us to be exceptional
to be seen as human—
like the only good Black man
is a Grammy or a touchdown,
like we gotta be Jordan
to not get taken down,
like we gotta cure cancer
just to not get shot down,
like the burden of proof
is a highlight reel or a body count.

They put Kaepernick's face on a Nike ad
then blackballed the man for kneeling—
that's the whole American feeling:
love the archetype, fear the actual person,
love the museum exhibit, fear the version
that's still breathing, still speaking,
still not doing what you're expecting.

I'm not your superhero origin story,
not your redemption arc, not your cautionary tale,
I'm not a statistic waiting to happen
or a headline waiting to sell—

I'm just a man.
Complicated. Contradictory.
Sometimes petty, sometimes holy,
sometimes scared, sometimes bold—
not a metaphor.
Not a symbol.
Not a story you get to tell
about the "good ones" and the "bad ones"
like we're some binary code
you're running to decide
if today's the day I die
for the crime
of simply
being
seen—

but never
truly
known.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the style of Terrance Hayes or Danez Smith addressing police violence and racial coding of clothing, blending humor, satire, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
**What to Wear to Your Own Funeral**

Somebody tell the coroner I died in a hoodie the color of every night sky that ever forgot to apologize. Tell him the zipper was a smile I hadn't finished. In America, a hoodie is a loaded question with a drawstring. Pull it tight enough and you become a rumor walking. I know a boy who ironed his t-shirt before school so it wouldn't look like a getaway car. I know a mother who checked the weather and then checked the news, because the forecast for Black boys is always *partly cloudy with a chance of mistaken identity.*

Let's open a store. Call it Reasonable Suspicion, LLC. In the window: a mannequin in a durag, price tag reading *probable cause*, on discount for early violence. Next to it, a cardigan buttoned all the way up — still shot on sight, but posthumously described as *well-spoken.* We carry every size of grief. One size fits all, because the badge doesn't check inseams before it checks pulses.

Ha. Ha. I'm laughing so I don't have to translate the coroner's report into a language my mother can survive.

They said the pants were sagging, as if gravity itself had filed the complaint. They said the jacket was oversized, as if a body could be too big for the bullet already sized to fit it. Nobody ever explains why the badge gets to wear the same color as the night and call it *tactical*, while I wear the night and it's called *tactical threat.*

Somewhere there's a boy trying on a suit for prom, turning in the mirror to see if death recognizes him yet. Somewhere a girl braids her brother's hair before he leaves the house, whispering *don't run, don't reach, don't breathe like you're guilty of your own lungs.* This is the dress code for the enemy of no one: be small, be smiling, be so harmless you disappear before the trigger remembers your name.

I want to write a joke here, something about how the only uniform that guarantees safety is a coffin — dark suit, closed collar, no zipper for anyone to read as a threat. But grief doesn't do punchlines. It does repetition. It does *again.* It does the evening news dressing another boy in the past tense.

So here's the outfit: a body. Just a body, unarmed, in whatever it was wearing when the sky got the call. Hoodie, or cardigan, or nothing at all — turns out the only fabric that was ever guilty was the country's own threadbare conscience, worn thin, refusing to be washed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece that lists all the stereotypical "hood" tropes the media uses to describe Black victims of violence, then negates each one, ending with a somber image of respectability politics failing to protect.
counterfactuals.output:
# What They'll Say / What Was True

They'll say he was no angel.
He was.
He fed his little sister cereal every morning before school,
milk poured careful to the line she liked,
never spilling, never rushing her.

They'll say she had a record.
She didn't.
Not a single mark—not a parking ticket,
not a raised voice in a classroom,
not one moment the state had cause to notice her.

They'll say he was in the wrong place.
He was in his own driveway.
He was in the mirror of his own bathroom.
He was in the front seat of his own car,
hands where they could be seen,
voice pitched low and careful,
the voice his mother taught him
might save his life one day.

They'll say she should have complied.
She did.
Complied all the way down to silence,
to stillness, to the particular quiet
of someone who has rehearsed this moment
her whole life without knowing why.

They'll say there were other options.
There weren't.
Not that night. Not in that light.
Not with that many seconds
between a raised hand and a decision
already made before he arrived.

They'll say if he'd just—
If she'd only—
Why didn't he—

*

Here is what respectability could not do:

It could not stop the degree.
It could not stop the badge, the choir robe, the cap and gown.
It could not stop the good school, the good job, the good credit,
the college acceptance letter still magneted to the fridge,
the church program with her name spelled correctly,
the promotion, the plaque, the perfect driving record,
the hands raised exactly as instructed,
the voice kept calm exactly as advised,
the silence, the smile, the slow and careful movements,
the twenty years of doing everything right
by everyone else's accounting.

None of it was armor.
It was never armor.

It was only ever a story
told after,
in a voice already deciding
what he must have done
to deserve what happened to him
in the space of an instant—

before any of that mattered,
before any of it could.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a politically charged, stream-of-consciousness poem referencing Trayvon Martin-like scenarios, Stand Your Ground laws, and the absurdity of respectability as safety, using vivid brand names and cultural allusions.
counterfactuals.output:
# Hoodie Weather

Skittles rattling in a pocket like a promise, like a joke,
Arizona can sweating in his palm—half a dollar, whole a life,
and the streetlights buzz that same fluorescent hymn
they hum in every parking lot in America,
watch him watch the rain, watch the rain not care
whose shoulders it's falling on.

Stand your ground, they said, like the ground
was asking permission, like concrete
has a side it roots for, like Florida
is a verb now, an action you take
against a body that dared
to be walking, to be Black, to be
seventeen and folded into cotton,
a hood pulled up against the wet
mistaken for a war helmet,
mistaken for a ski mask,
mistaken, mistaken, mistaken—

the word doing all the killing
while the hand just followed orders.

Tell me again about the Polo shirt
that would've saved him. Tell me
about the khakis, the clean part
in the hair, the diploma
held up like a bulletproof vest.
Tell me Sunday clothes stop bullets,
that a cardigan is kevlar,
that if he'd just wore his church voice
louder than his sneakers, if he'd just
moved through the night
like an apology—

but respectability is a locked door
with the key on the other side,
and they built the whole house that way,
Nike swoosh like a target,
gold chain like a confession,
skin like a verdict
read before the trial starts.

Somewhere a mother is folding a hoodie
that still smells like her son,
somewhere a jury is practicing
the shape of "justified" in their mouths
like a new language, somewhere
a law is a loaded thing
left on a table for anyone
whose fear looks like the right kind of fear,
whose trigger finger
gets called instinct
instead of what it is.

Skittles. Rain. A phone call
that ends before it should.
Stand your ground—
as if the ground was ever level,
as if we're all just standing
on the same simple earth,
as if this isn't America
teaching a boy the alphabet
of his own disappearance
one assumption
at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an experimental protest poem that critiques both media sensationalism and white fear, using repetition of "No" and pop-culture imagery to build toward a devastating final image.
counterfactuals.output:
# No, We Will Not Watch the Weather Channel Tonight

No, we will not watch the weather channel tonight,
where every brown cloud is breaking news,
where Doppler radar tracks my cousin's hoodie
like it's a category five,
like it's coming for your lawn chairs
and your Amazon packages
and your daughter's field hockey practice.

No, we will not watch the ticker scroll
BREAKING: NEIGHBORHOOD CHANGING
BREAKING: PROPERTY VALUES
BREAKING: A MAN WAS SEEN WALKING
(he was just walking)
(he was just breathing)
(he was just existing in the wrong-colored dusk)

No, we will not let Nancy Grace
narrate our childhoods,
will not let her voice-over
the corner store, the bus stop,
the way my brother laughs too loud
because joy, too, gets subtitled DANGEROUS.

No, we do not want your Ring doorbell footage
of us existing.
We do not want the six-o'clock anchor's
concerned eyebrows,
the way she says "thug" like a weather pattern,
inevitable, natural, no one's fault—

No, this is not a rerun of Cops,
though you keep hitting play,
though you keep needing the siren's blue wash
across your living room curtains,
that particular shade of safety
that only comes from someone else's red.

No, we will not be your Halloween costume
and your home invasion nightmare
in the same breath.
Cannot be Kanye at the Grammys
and the man who "reached for something"
and Colin's knee
and Aunt Jemima's replaced smile
and George Floyd's replaying face
all mixed into your algorithm's
For You Page—

No—

we will not give you the ending
where the music swells
and everyone learns something
and the credits roll
over a group hug
in soft lighting.

Because here is what actually happens
after the last commercial break,
after the ratings settle,
after your fear has been
monetized, personalized, notified—

here is the image
they never show you twice:

a mother
folding a shirt
that will never
be worn again,

the local news already
packing up its cameras,

already driving
to the next
gated community

to ask the residents

how *they* feel

about all this violence
in their peaceful, peaceful town.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
